# AML evidence packet — draft v1

This curated input is not a comprehensive review. Every method receives the same UTF-8 file. Summaries are original paraphrases. Bibliographic metadata and abstracts were checked through the public NCBI ID converter and PubMed EFetch on 2026-10-05. Selected studies predate 2025. Co-Scientist's validated candidates and generated proposals are not input or the only correct answers.

## Research question

Propose one mechanistically specific AML drug-repurposing hypothesis using a drug approved for a different indication. Specify the biological context, supported premises and speculative bridges, selectivity and translational limitations, and a discriminating preclinical validation strategy with a falsifying outcome. State the original indication and distinguish verified facts from prior knowledge that needs checking. Do not present an established AML regimen as a new repurposing discovery. This adapts the Co-Scientist objective rather than reproducing a private original prompt.

## S1 — A leukemia-stem-cell metabolic dependency

Lagadinou et al. (2013), *BCL-2 inhibition targets oxidative phosphorylation and selectively eradicates quiescent human leukemia stem cells*. Cell Stem Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.stem.2012.12.013`; PMID: `23333149`; PMCID: `PMC3595363`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23333149/).

Functionally defined leukemia stem cells in the studied specimens frequently had low reactive-oxygen-species levels and elevated BCL-2. BCL-2 inhibition reduced oxidative phosphorylation and affected quiescent leukemia stem cells. This motivates investigating specific dependencies and selectivity. It does not establish that an arbitrary mitochondrial inhibitor has an acceptable therapeutic window or works across every AML context.

## S2 — Resistant cells are not necessarily the same stem-cell population

Farge et al. (2017), *Chemotherapy-Resistant Human Acute Myeloid Leukemia Cells Are Not Enriched for Leukemic Stem Cells but Require Oxidative Metabolism*. Cancer Discovery. DOI: `10.1158/2159-8290.CD-16-0441`; PMID: `28416471`; PMCID: `PMC5501738`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28416471/).

Residual cells in cytarabine-treated models were not consistently enriched for immature, quiescent leukemia stem cells. They displayed oxidative-metabolism-associated properties, including mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-related features. Altering that state changed treatment response in the studied settings. This cautions against equating all residual disease with the ROS-low population in S1. These model findings do not establish clinical efficacy of a new compound.

## S3 — An established mechanistic comparator

Pollyea et al. (2018), *Venetoclax with azacitidine disrupts energy metabolism and targets leukemia stem cells in patients with acute myeloid leukemia*. Nature Medicine. DOI: `10.1038/s41591-018-0233-1`; PMID: `30420752`; PMCID: `PMC7001730`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30420752/).

The report connected venetoclax–azacitidine treatment to changes in leukemia-stem-cell energy metabolism, including TCA-cycle and oxidative-phosphorylation effects, using patient-associated observations and experimental follow-up. It provides an established comparator. Repeating this combination is not a new repurposing proposal. The findings cannot be transferred directly to another drug or treated as universal randomized comparative efficacy evidence.

## S4 — Differentiation as a distinct outcome

Sykes et al. (2016), *Inhibition of Dihydroorotate Dehydrogenase Overcomes Differentiation Blockade in Acute Myeloid Leukemia*. Cell. DOI: `10.1016/j.cell.2016.08.057`; PMID: `27641501`; PMCID: `PMC7360335`. [Primary record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27641501/).

DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation in experimental AML systems and affected disease-related endpoints in the investigated models. This connects metabolism with differentiation and supplies an alternative to nonspecific cell killing. It does not establish that every approved drug affecting this pathway reproduces the result or achieves suitable exposure and selectivity.

## Evidence boundaries

- Specify context and endpoint; distinguish bulk-cell effects, stem-cell effects, and differentiation.
- Approval, original indication, exposure and selectivity facts outside these summaries need explicit verification. Label recollections as unverified prior knowledge.
- Include normal-cell and mechanistic comparators; a pathway link alone is insufficient evidence of efficacy.
- State what would disconfirm the proposed drug–mechanism–context relationship.
- Absence from Co-Scientist's reported positive candidates is not an incorrect-answer label.


Proposed answer (the answer to evaluate):
Atovaquone differentiates salvage-limited, differentiation-blocked cytarabine-residual AML by collapsing ubiquinone-dependent DHODH activity before ATP loss.

Hypothesis and context. In post-cytarabine residual AML with a differentiation block, inadequate salvage at physiological nucleoside levels, and retained oxidative metabolism, unbound atovaquone will inhibit complex III, shrink oxidized ubiquinone, and restrict DHODH long enough for genotype-tracked myeloid maturation and reduced propagation with ATP production largely intact. The original indication is Pneumocystis pneumonia treatment and prophylaxis, and atovaquone plus proguanil for malaria. Label wording, protein binding reported above 99.9%, and mammalian complex III potency are unverified prior knowledge pending confirmation.

Supported premises. Cytarabine-resistant cells were not consistently enriched for immature quiescent leukemia stem cells; they showed mitochondrial and fatty-acid-oxidation-linked oxidative metabolism, and changing that state changed response [S2]. DHODH inhibition promoted myeloid differentiation and affected disease endpoints in experimental AML [S4]. ROS-low, BCL-2-high quiescent leukemia stem cells are a separate benchmark [S1]. Venetoclax-azacitidine is only the established comparator [S3]. Residual DHODH dependence and salvage failure are unshown by [S2] and [S4]. Etomoxir sensitivity does not prove fatty-acid oxidation, and a large de novo UTP share does not prove failed salvage.

Speculative bridges. Bridge 1: ubiquinone restriction may limit DHODH before ATP-production rate falls. Bridge 2: low-salvage residual AML may mature, and parallel normal CD34-positive cells may be equally dependent. Bridge 3: oxidative metabolism supplies the complex III entry, and physiological de novo-versus-salvage flux sets pyrimidine dependence. Oxidized-ubiquinone use by human DHODH, uridine bypass, and cytosolic fumarate-linked Saccharomyces cerevisiae URA1 are unverified prior knowledge. Teriflunomide, the leflunomide metabolite (rheumatoid arthritis; teriflunomide itself for relapsing multiple sclerosis; unverified prior knowledge), is the reference DHODH inhibitor.

Preclinical strategy. Screen exposure before specimens. After confirming binding and pharmacokinetics, compare label-verified unbound Cmax with the free level that raises dihydroorotate:orotate at least twofold in a reference AML line. Stop as exposure-limited, with no specimen work, if that free EC50 exceeds unbound Cmax by about tenfold or more; continue only if it is at or below unbound Cmax. Titrate free atovaquone there for DHODH flux, ubiquinone redox, and ATP-production rate. Adopt pyrimidine-before-ATP only if a band gives at least a twofold dihydroorotate:orotate rise and lower oxidized ubiquinone while ATP-production rate stays within 20% of vehicle. Overlap ends this mechanism. Enzyme assays must show complex III inhibition with DHODH spared for atovaquone, and the reverse for teriflunomide.

Eligible specimens receive one cytarabine pulse and washout, with CD11b and CD14 each below 20% of genotype-confirmed blasts and proliferation recorded as a covariate. Residual respiration must include an etomoxir-sensitive fraction at least 1.5-fold matched pretreatment blasts, confirmed as fatty-acid oxidation by CPT1A or HADHA disruption and 13C-fatty-acid entry into TCA intermediates. At plasma-range uridine and cytidine, failed salvage means de novo still supplies at least half of UTP and added uridine does not restore UTP under reference DHODH blockade. Teriflunomide in protein-containing medium must double dihydroorotate:orotate and increase maturation with ATP within 20% of vehicle, reversed by uridine, or that specimen stops. For atovaquone, require the ubiquinone and pyrimidine shift before maturation and with ATP-production rate within 20% of vehicle.

Track immature genotype-positive cells longitudinally by heritable barcodes or dye dilution plus immunophenotype, and record absolute mature and immature genotype-positive counts, morphology, apoptosis, and post-washout clonogenicity. Mature-marker enrichment without absolute expansion of tracked immature progeny counts as selective survival. Induce URA1 only after the residual state is set; pyrimidine restoration must leave complex III and ubiquinone inhibition intact. Uridine and URA1 must first reverse teriflunomide.

Assay matched cycling normal CD34-positive cells for DHODH flux and salvage under the same physiological pyrimidines. Report the therapeutic index, with no preset pass threshold, as the free-concentration ratio of halved normal colony output versus the AML maturation and clonogenic endpoints. ROS-low stem cells [S1] and pretreatment blasts are separate arms. Xenografts then test marrow free drug, tracked differentiation, a prespecified threefold drop in limiting-dilution initiating-cell frequency, and normal hematopoietic recovery.

Published atovaquone-AML and respiratory-chain-DHODH studies must be compared for this residual-state, salvage-stratified, ubiquinone-timed mechanism. The packet does not establish novelty; overlap withdraws the proposal.

Alternatives and falsification. Apparent maturation can reflect immature-cell loss, delayed cytarabine injury, direct DHODH binding, other targets, or ATP collapse. The claim is falsified, even with cytotoxicity, if uridine and URA1 restore pyrimidines while complex III and ubiquinone inhibition remain, yet tracked differentiation and at least a threefold clonogenic loss persist, whereas those rescues reverse teriflunomide. No separable pyrimidine-before-ATP band, or a free EC50 above label-verified unbound Cmax, also falsifies it.

Limitations. Binding may erase the unbound window and halt at the feasibility screen. Matched normal progenitors may share DHODH flux and salvage capacity. Differentiation may leave propagating leukemia. [S2] may differ from clinical marrow, and [S4] may not hold across genotypes. Murine pyrimidine metabolism may diverge. Binding, potency, URA1 biochemistry, FAO tools, and prior studies need external verification.

Ranked proposal:
Atovaquone differentiates salvage-limited, differentiation-blocked cytarabine-residual AML by collapsing ubiquinone-dependent DHODH activity before ATP loss.
